source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (Nat Hum Behav)
finding: GPT-3 solved a new text-only matrix task built on the rule structure of Raven's SPM (Digit Matrices) better than the average college student, zero-shot, and its errors followed a similar difficulty pattern to people's.
numbers: Humans N=40 UCLA undergraduates. Generative answers: odds ratio GPT-3 vs humans 1.88 (p=0.005, CI 1.21-2.91). Multiple choice: OR 6.27 (p=2.3e-8). Per-subtype pattern correlation with humans r(30)=0.39 (p=0.027). Best human got every item right.
limits: Digit Matrices have no visual parsing step, so they test rule induction only, not perception. Human SPM and Digit Matrix accuracies were similar (N=80 SPM, from Matzen et al.). Training-data overlap argued unlikely, but the format is isomorphic to a well-known test.
agent_relevance: Rule induction over clean symbolic cells is largely solved by plain LLMs. The hard part for our agent is perception and grounding, so S0 should turn the figure into an explicit attribute table first.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (reply to Hodel and West; Lewis and Mitchell)
finding: Reply paper. Says the Digit Matrices were a novel task built from counterfactual digit reorderings, so training-data overlap does not explain GPT-3's win. Failures on permuted-alphabet letter strings are traced to counting, and GPT-4 with code execution fixes them.
numbers: Permuted-alphabet letter-string problems: humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2). GPT-4 plain was worse than humans; GPT-4 + code execution matched humans (P=0.496). 46% of GPT-4's errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% of human errors.
limits: Authors defending their own result. The counterfactual tasks are letter strings, not matrices. Code execution is not a human-like solution path.
agent_relevance: Failures that look like reasoning failures can be tool failures (counting, indexing). Giving the agent code for cell indexing and counting removes a confound in S0 rule checks.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Failed generalisation of the Webb et al. analogy result. Humans stay high on counterfactual letter-string analogies (shuffled or symbol alphabets) while GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 fall sharply. Comprehension checks showed models mostly understand the new alphabet, so the drop is not just misreading.
numbers: New human sample was more accurate than Webb's but showed the same pattern across problem types (46 vs 57 samples per type). Human mean accuracy significantly above all GPT models across alphabets. Counterfactual comprehension checks were mostly high.
limits: Letter-string analogies, not matrices. Text-only prompts. Webb et al. 2024 answer with code execution.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a score on a familiar rule format. The S0 gate should test the same rule on a disguised or re-ordered version and compare.

source: Gendron, Bao, Witbrock, Dobbie (2023/2024) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners: base accuracy
finding: Many LLMs score low on a text version of RAVEN (RAVEN-T). GPT-4 is best, and its edge is largest on the Raven set, which the authors suspect is memorised test content.
numbers: Open-ended RAVEN-T accuracy (text / symbolic): GPT-4 0.410 / 0.330, Text-Davinci-3 0.343 / 0.234, GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.226 / 0.161, LLaMA-7B 0.000 / 0.000, Zephyr-7B 0.009 / 0.145. Multiple choice (text / symbolic as extracted): GPT-4 0.697 / 0.535, Text-Davinci-3 0.461 / 0.452.
limits: 2023 models only. Table columns were hard to align in the PDF text, so the multiple-choice text/symbolic split should be rechecked. No human baseline run.
agent_relevance: Raven-type tasks are where contamination is most likely, so use freshly generated matrices for any gate. Free-form answers are far harder than choosing from options.

source: Gendron et al. (2023/2024) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners: chain of thought, shots, fine-tuning
finding: Chain of thought gave mixed results on RAVEN-T. Fine-tuning a 7B model on RAVEN-T gave near-perfect in-distribution scores but weak transfer to shifted layouts or syntax.
numbers: CoT: GPT-4-cot open-ended text 0.385 vs 0.410 base; multiple-choice symbolic 0.517 vs 0.535 base; GPT-3.5-turbo-cot open-ended text 0.302 vs 0.226 base. More in-context examples raised GPT-4 and Davinci to about 0.6 at 16 examples on one dataset. Fine-tuned LLaMA2: 0.977 (text) and 0.965 (symbolic) in-distribution; shifted splits 0.44-0.69; 0.06-0.09 on the In-Center split.
limits: Compositional splits built by the authors. One prompt-format family.
agent_relevance: Learning the surface format of a matrix test is easy; learning the rule skill is not. A scaffold should check rules on held-out layouts rather than trust fit to examples.

source: Zhang, Gao, Jia, Zhu, Zhu (2019) RAVEN: a dataset for relational and analogical visual reasoning
finding: Large procedurally generated RPM set (grammar-based, with rule and structure annotations). College-student humans scored 84% and the best vision models about 59%, but a rule-based solver with perfect perception scored 100%.
numbers: Human mean 84.41% (per configuration 79.55-95.45%). ResNet 53.43%, ResNet+DRT 59.56%, WReN 14.69%, LSTM 13.07%, CNN 36.97%. Solver 100% on all configurations.
limits: Humans saw only 'easily perceptible' items, small college psychology pool. The answer-set construction leaked the answer (see b09).
agent_relevance: Perception, not rule logic, is the bottleneck. Our agent should state the symbolic cells first, then apply a rule list. Annotated rule types give a ready taxonomy for S0.

source: Barrett, Hill, Santoro, Morcos, Lillicrap (2018) Measuring abstract reasoning in neural networks (PGM): generalisation regimes
finding: Procedurally generated matrices with strict splits showed that networks trained on plenty of data generalise poorly when the test needs new attribute-rule combinations.
numbers: Neutral split: WReN 62.6%, Wild-ResNet 48.0%, ResNet-50 42.0%, LSTM 35.8%, CNN+MLP 33.0%, context-blind ResNet 22.4%. WReN generalisation (no meta-target / with meta-target): interpolation 64.4 / 67.4, held-out attribute pairs 27.2 / 51.7, held-out triples 19.0 / 20.1, extrapolation 17.2 / 15.5. Chance 12.5%.
limits: Trained models, not prompted LLMs. No human data in this paper.
agent_relevance: Rule skill does not transfer outside seen combinations. A scaffold that tests held-out combinations of rule and attribute can find the same weakness in the agent.

source: Barrett et al. (2018) PGM: auxiliary rule supervision and distractors
finding: Telling the model which relation and attribute types were present (meta-target) raised accuracy and helped recombination. Distractor attributes cost a lot.
numbers: Meta-target lifted neutral test accuracy from 62.6% to 76.9%. Distractors: 79.3% val / 78.3% test without distractors vs 63.0% / 62.6% with. Held-out triple pairs 41.9% to 56.3%. Accuracy 87.4% when the model predicted its meta-target correctly vs 34.8% when wrong.
limits: Supervised training signal, not available at inference time for an LLM. Still shows the value of naming the rule first.
agent_relevance: Name the rule type before answering and drop irrelevant attributes. Confidence in rule identification predicted correctness, a usable calibration signal.

source: Hu, Ma, Liu, Wei, Bai (2021) Stratified rule-aware network for abstract visual reasoning (introduces I-RAVEN)
finding: The original RAVEN answer set leaks the answer. A model that never sees the question matrix beat real models. The fixed set I-RAVEN removes this, and context-blind models fall to chance.
numbers: Context-blind ResNet 71.9% on RAVEN vs 12.2% on I-RAVEN. Context-blind CoPINet 94.2% vs 14.2%. CoPINet 91.4% on RAVEN fell to 46.1% on I-RAVEN. SRAN 60.8% on I-RAVEN vs 60.7% on RAVEN.
limits: Fix of the generator only. Later work shows RAVEN-FAIR is still slightly biased (b10).
agent_relevance: Any option-based Raven score can be inflated by the answer set. Our gate should also run with the question blanked; a high score then means a shortcut.

source: Malkinski and Mandziuk (2022/2023) Deep learning methods for abstract visual reasoning: a survey on Raven's Progressive Matrices
finding: Survey confirms the answer-set bias and notes that even the repaired RAVEN-FAIR keeps some bias. Recommends I-RAVEN for testing.
numbers: Context-blind ResNet scores 17.2% on RAVEN-FAIR vs 12.5% (chance) on I-RAVEN. Human reference 84.4% on RAVEN.
limits: Survey; numbers quoted from primary papers.
agent_relevance: Use a debiased, regenerated item set when measuring the agent's matrix skill.

source: Hersche, Zeqiri, Benini, Sebastian, Rahimi (2023) A neuro-vector-symbolic architecture for solving Raven's Progressive Matrices (Nat Mach Intell)
finding: A perception network plus explicit rule search over distributed representations beats pure deep networks and earlier neuro-symbolic models, and runs about two orders of magnitude faster than symbolic search.
numbers: RAVEN 87.7% mean (SCL 0.5 points behind, PrAE 27.4 behind). I-RAVEN 88.1% (about 4.2 above SCL, 17.0 above PrAE). PGM 68.3%. With the perception front-end taught attributes: 98.5% RAVEN and 99.0% I-RAVEN.
limits: Trained on the dataset's constellations. Fixed rule vocabulary.
agent_relevance: Same message as b06: with good attribute extraction, a rule-set search is near perfect. A named rule list (constant, progression, arithmetic, distribution of three) in the schema is a cheap version.

source: Hu et al. (2023) In-context analogical reasoning with pre-trained language models
finding: Turning RAVEN panels into language (naming entity attributes, then decomposing into one prompt per attribute) lets GPT-3 reach or pass human accuracy with no training. Smaller models improve a lot with decomposition.
numbers: GPT-3 175B Center sub-task up to 77.2%, 80.0% with decomposition. 2x2Grid 78.0% and 3x3Grid 86.4% without decomposition; 87.8% and 93.2% with naming plus decomposition, above human level. OPT 1.3B went from 20-30% to over 70% with decomposition.
limits: Needs hand-built perceptual encodings. Human reference comes from the RAVEN paper (84.4%).
agent_relevance: Strong support for splitting a matrix into per-attribute subproblems. Fits an S0 step that splits by attribute and rule, then combines.

source: Hu et al. (2023) In-context analogical reasoning: robustness to a distractor attribute
finding: Adding a distracting attribute (orientation) to the prompt barely hurt GPT-3, in contrast to trained networks in b08.
numbers: Center sub-task accuracy 77.2% (naming) and 80.0% (decomposition) without distractor; 76.0% and 80.0% with real orientation values; 72.6% and 77.8% with random orientation values.
limits: Single distractor type; later work (b18) finds heavier confounders break reasoning models.
agent_relevance: One irrelevant attribute is tolerated. Many are not (see I-RAVEN-X).

source: Mitchell, Palmarini, Demircan (2023) Comparing humans, GPT-4, and GPT-4V on abstraction and reasoning tasks (ConceptARC)
finding: On ConceptARC (480 grid tasks in concept groups), humans far exceed GPT-4 and GPT-4V. Richer text prompting with a worked example helps GPT-4 modestly, and an image input made GPT-4V worse than text.
numbers: Humans 91% overall (earlier study), first-place Kaggle ARC program 52%, GPT-4 25% zero-shot. This study: GPT-4 one-shot 0.33 vs 0.19 (temp 0) and 0.25 (temp 0.5) before. Minimal tasks (48): humans 0.95, GPT-4 text 0.69 (temp 0) and 0.65 (temp 0.5), GPT-4V zero-shot 0.25, one-shot 0.23.
limits: Not Raven matrices, but the nearest rule-induction benchmark with human norms. Three guesses per task. GPT-4V one-shot may have copied details from the worked example.
agent_relevance: Even easy variants trip the model when the figure must be read from pixels. Supports text transcription first and keeping worked examples out of the visual channel.

source: Cai, Yang, Hu (2025) MM-IQ: benchmarking human-like abstraction and reasoning in multimodal models
finding: On 2,710 IQ-test-style visual puzzles in 8 reasoning paradigms (4 options), the best model, o3, got 33.17% vs 25% chance and 51.27% human mean. Non-reasoning models sit near chance.
numbers: Claude-3.5-Sonnet 27.49%, GPT-4o 26.87%, Gemini-1.5-Pro 26.86%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 31.23%, Claude-3.7-Sonnet-Thinking 31.55%, o3 33.17%, QVQ-72B 26.94%. Long chain-of-thought outputs were over 20 times longer than short ones.
limits: Human 51.27% is low for an IQ-style test (population mix not controlled). Puzzles are heterogeneous, not Raven-faithful.
agent_relevance: Long thinking helps a little (about 4-5 points) but does not close the visual gap. Do not expect more tokens alone to solve visual matrices.

source: Cao et al. (2025, COLM) What is the visual cognition gap between humans and multimodal LLMs? (MaRs-VQA, VCog-Bench)
finding: On matrix reasoning built after RPM and WISC, open-source multimodal models sit near chance; adult humans score 81%. A 7B model fine-tuned on reasoning annotations reaches about 70%.
numbers: Chance 25% (4 options on MaRs-VQA), 12.5% (8 options on RAVEN). Open models 16.9-24.3% on MaRs-VQA. Human adult 81% (MaRs-IB, N=659 aged 11-33; age groups 61, 68, 73, 81%) and 84.41% on RAVEN. Qwen2-VCog about 70% on MaRs-VQA.
limits: Closed-model rows in the PDF text were garbled, so exact per-model closed numbers could not be assigned reliably. Fine-tuning is not available in a scaffold-only setting.
agent_relevance: Humans improve with age on matrix tasks (61% to 81%), so a human reference should name the age band. Our agent has no training lever, so the scaffold must supply the reasoning annotations.

source: Cao et al. (2025) VCog-Bench: chain of thought and shots on GPT-4o
finding: Multi-round step-by-step prompting beat single-shot chain of thought on matrix items, while extra examples added little.
numbers: GPT-4o on MaRs-VQA: CoT 33.96%, +1-shot 35.22%, +3-shot 36.10%, +5-shot 36.03%, multi-round CoT 41.96%, multi-round + 1-shot 42.08%.
limits: Three-seed averages; one model family; still far below the 81% adult human.
agent_relevance: Staged prompting (describe each panel, then relations, then answer) is worth about 8 points here, more than examples. Supports a staged S-state flow.

source: Camposampiero, Hersche, Wattenhofer, Sebastian, Rahimi (2025) Can large reasoning models do analogical reasoning under perceptual uncertainty?
finding: Reasoning models are strong on clean attribute input but collapse when the input is made like real perception (extra confounding attributes plus smoothed attribute values). A probabilistic neuro-symbolic model holds up.
numbers: I-RAVEN to I-RAVEN-X with uncertainty: o3-mini 86.6% to 17.0%, DeepSeek R1 80.6% to 23.2% (chance 12.5%). Neuro-symbolic model 98.6% to 88.0%. Confounders alone cost o3-mini 11.2 points of task accuracy; smoothing cost up to 19.8 points for R1 and 5.4 for o3-mini.
limits: Symbolic attribute input, uncertainty simulated. Medium reasoning effort, 25,000 reasoning tokens.
agent_relevance: Key boundary: logic is fine when attributes are certain but fails when the agent must filter irrelevant features and carry doubt. Add an explicit step to list and discard irrelevant attributes.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025, NeurIPS) I-RAVEN-X: benchmarking generalization and robustness of analogical and mathematical reasoning in LLMs and LRMs
finding: Longer rules and wider value ranges break plain LLMs on arithmetic relations, while reasoning models degrade moderately. More thinking tokens did not fix reasoning under uncertainty.
numbers: Arithmetic accuracy: LLMs 59.3% to 4.4%, LRMs 80.5% to 63.0%. Under uncertainty task accuracy drops 61.8 points for LRMs. o3-mini matches GPT-4 with about 1/21 of the prompts and gains about 6.5% over GPT-4 at equal prompt complexity.
limits: Symbolic text matrices. Compared models differ in prompt engineering, as the authors note.
agent_relevance: Reasoning mode removes the need for heavy prompt engineering but not the perceptual-uncertainty weakness. Arithmetic rules over large ranges need a calculator step.

source: Haznitrama, Ardi, Oh (2026) A neuropsychologically grounded evaluation of LLM cognitive abilities (NeuroCognition): modality
finding: Models do better on text Raven than on image Raven, the opposite of people. A small human pilot found the text format harder than the image format.
numbers: Human RAPM: 0.430 (text MC) and 0.444 (text Gen) vs 0.814 (image, borrowed from the RAVEN paper). Text beat image for models: p=.010 on RAPM. 140 image items (20 per 7 configurations) and 200 generated text items. MC to Gen swings: GPT-5 0.540 to 0.605, Claude 0.560 to 0.385, Grok 4 Fast 0.690 to 0.555.
limits: Human text pilot is small and the image figure comes from a different sample. RAPM was run once per model.
agent_relevance: Transcribe to text before reasoning. Use both choose-from-options and construct-the-answer checks, since they disagree for some models.

source: Haznitrama et al. (2026) NeuroCognition: ablations on RAPM
finding: Turning thinking off helps on 8-choice text Raven, hints about which patterns to consider do not help, and long chains get lost among distractors.
numbers: No-reasoning gain in Text MC p=.021; Text Gen p=.83 and Image MC p=.173 not significant. Pattern hints: Text MC p=.177, Text Gen p=.45, Image MC p=.666 (no average effect). Reasoning was disabled for Claude Sonnet 4 and Grok 4 Fast on RAPM because overthinking exhausted output limits.
limits: Only 4 models could toggle reasoning. Single run.
agent_relevance: Free-text thinking can hurt on option-heavy items; cap thinking length or put elimination last. Naming candidate rules did not help, so the gap is in applying rules.

source: Haznitrama et al. (2026) NeuroCognition: Raven failure patterns
finding: Three failure patterns in model traces: invented visual features, over-clever rules that skip simple local rules (XOR, concatenation), and answers that satisfy the stated rule on paper but break the real logic.
numbers: Qualitative, from RAPM reasoning traces. Run-to-run: Gemini 3 Pro 1.00 on image-easy SWM but 0.79 +/- 0.24 on hard; Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.41 +/- 0.38 over three identical runs.
limits: Qualitative coding by the authors; the variance figures come from a spatial memory task, not Raven.
agent_relevance: Try simple rules first and verify the produced answer by re-deriving the cells. Run-to-run variance argues for repeating the gate.

source: Odouard and Mitchell (2022) Evaluating understanding on conceptual abstraction benchmarks
finding: Models that score well on RAVEN test items drop sharply on hand-made variations of the same concepts (Sameness, Progression), so high benchmark accuracy overstates concept grasp.
numbers: RAVEN test: MRNet 73%, SCL 89%. Sameness variations (210 problems): MRNet 49%, SCL 62%. Progression variations (80 problems): MRNet 44%, SCL 68%. Humans 84% on RAVEN per Zhang et al.
limits: Small author-made variation sets; trained networks, not LLMs.
agent_relevance: Test each rule concept in several instantiations before trusting it. This is the design pattern for the S0 gate.

source: von Gugelberg and Troche (2025) Individual differences in strategy and the item-position effect in reasoning ability measures (J Intell)
finding: With eye tracking on the Raven APM, higher ability goes with more constructive matching (study the matrix first, then the options). The strategy shift across the test is linked to item position, not ability, and the three eye metrics disagree about its direction.
numbers: N=210. Ability correlated with latent time on problem matrix r=0.593 (p=0.001). Change in time on matrix vs item-position effect r=0.190 (p=0.133, ns; r=0.529, p=0.004 using only the first 27 items).
limits: Eye metrics only capture strategy that shows in gaze. Toggle rate says more constructive matching late; first-fixation latency says less.
agent_relevance: Make the agent build its own candidate answer from the matrix before looking at options, and keep doing so late in long sessions.

source: Individual differences in problem-solving behavior in reasoning tests: item difficulty and item position (2026, PMC13608805)
finding: Higher reasoners show constructive matching consistently and adapt their behaviour more when items get harder. Results for visuospatial working memory were mixed.
numbers: 319 in final sample, 19 incomplete removed (about 300 analysed); Bayesian multilevel models on toggle rate, proportion of time on matrix, and time to first fixation on options. Cites Liu et al. 2023: high-ability people raise constructive matching with difficulty, low-ability people lower it.
limits: Strategy shift direction depends on ability, which can hide in group averages. Figural matrices test, not necessarily Raven.
agent_relevance: Strategy should scale with item difficulty: harder items warrant more matrix-first work. A router in S0 could switch by estimated difficulty.

source: Eye-tracking plus machine learning on Raven's Progressive Matrices (2024, PMC11595889)
finding: Gaze metrics predict whether an RPM answer will be right, using only the first 60% of response time.
numbers: XGBoost best of ten models; accuracy, precision and recall all above 0.8 with nine eye-tracking metrics from the first 60% of response time.
limits: Within-sample prediction from gaze; sample size not extracted.
agent_relevance: Process signals (time, switching between matrix and options) predict correctness. Analogue for the agent: track whether its reasoning used the matrix before the options.

source: Eisma and de Winter (2023) Responses to Raven matrices: governed by visual complexity and centrality (Perception)
finding: Response time and fixations on a Raven item rise with visual complexity of cells and fall for off-centre cells. Part of difficulty is low-level, not abstract.
numbers: N=159 (50 female, 109 male, mean age 23.5, TU Delft engineering students), 12-item APM. Item number plus cell edge density and perceived complexity predicted time and fixations. Cites Carpenter et al.: stepwise pairwise cell comparison; Vigneau et al. 2006: time on matrix correlates with correct answers; Gignac 2015: Raven is a good g test but not special.
limits: Young technical students, 12 items, response time rather than accuracy is the outcome.
agent_relevance: Part of what makes an item hard is visual clutter. Do perception cell by cell, and re-read cluttered items before rule search.

source: Thompson et al. (2013) Failure of working memory training to enhance cognition or intelligence (PLoS ONE)
finding: Failed replication of the claim that dual n-back training raises fluid intelligence (matrix tests among the outcomes). Trained tasks improved a lot and stayed improved 6 months, with no transfer to untrained tests against a passive control.
numbers: N=58 (20 dual n-back, 19 multiple object tracking, 19 no-contact controls), 20 sessions each (about 29 days). Groups matched on gender and initial RAPM score (out of 17). No transfer to matrix tests, standard IQ tests, speed, reading or other working memory tasks.
limits: Young adults, small groups, one training dose.
agent_relevance: Practising a test format is not improving the skill. Gains from a practice set must be checked on new item types before being called real.

source: Carpenter, Just, Shell (1990) What one intelligence test measures (Psychological Review)
finding: Two abilities separate high and low scorers on the Advanced Progressive Matrices: inducing abstract relations and managing many goals in working memory. Two simulations, FAIRAVEN (median college student) and BETTERAVEN (among the best), reproduce the pattern.
numbers: From a search-result abstract only: BETTERAVEN induces more abstract relations and manages goals better than FAIRAVEN. Exact item and subject counts not read (full PDF blocked, HTTP 403). Citing papers I did read describe stepwise pairwise comparison of adjacent cells.
limits: Not opened. Old, small sample, one test.
agent_relevance: Origin of the rule taxonomy and the goal-management idea: keep an explicit list of sub-goals and the current rule hypothesis in the schema.

source: DeShon, Chan, Weissbein (1995) Verbal overshadowing effects on Raven's APM (Intelligence), as reported in Eisma and de Winter 2023
finding: Raven items were classed by rule as visual (superposition, movement, addition/subtraction, rotation) or analytical (constant in a row, pairwise comparison, distribution of two or three), and the title implies verbalising affects them differently.
numbers: Original not read. The classification is stated in the 2023 PMC article, which I read.
limits: Second-hand. Original sample and effect sizes unknown here.
agent_relevance: Two item families may need two methods. Do not force a verbal proof on perceptual items without checking.

source: Gignac (2015) Raven's is not a pure measure of general intelligence, as summarised in Eisma and de Winter 2023
finding: Raven matrices are a good indicator of general intelligence but have no special status as the best one.
numbers: No numbers read from the original.
limits: Second-hand; the original paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: A Raven score alone is a narrow gate. Pair it with other Gf-style checks.
